# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-21 (Extended v156)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826; **current narrative point (late evening 24th June 1832)**: Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house with secret passage to Rue de Babylone), Place de la Bastille (elephant monument under construction), Prison Charlemagne (Fine-Air top story), Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile (ruin wall), Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire No. 6 (Gillenormand residence), English provincial towns (Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford). **Seasonal progression**: Winter Year 5 (frost, rain, thunder, muddy roads, early darkness) transitioned to spring Year 6 (cholera decimated Paris during spring). **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Yera Stenworth confided that fire at Dunstead granary was set deliberately—unverified. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Fenelle Lindmere confided that Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family—unverified. **Rumor (current period)**: Second daughter of Rorald Lindmere spread rumor that Pelde Stenworth died of plague—unverified.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (Autumn Year 5—Late June 1832)
**The wound**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn (origin unclear). Detained one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette devoted herself entirely to his care. Recovered through March-April.

**Mysterious journeys and nocturnal manuscript**: Valjean took occasional journeys of one or two days, destination unknown to Cosette, typically when money lacking. Cosette observed figure walking in garden dusk carrying large club. Found stone on bench; became alarmed. Later discovered packet of philosophical manuscript on bench—meditation on love as divine spark. **Cosette recognized writer as Marius.**

**Imminent departure (late June 1832)**: Valjean told Cosette morning of 24th June that he must settle all affairs; hold herself in readiness; he will give her linen to pack in trunk; obliged to go on journey; they are to go away; large trunk needed for her and small one for him. All to be ready in one week. **Possible destination: England.** Resumed carrying bread to hungry, clothing to cold; Cosette often accompanied him.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (Autumn Year 5—Late June 1832)
**Recognition and revelation**: Upon reading manuscript, Cosette acknowledged she had never truly forgotten Marius, had always loved and adored him. "The fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it burst forth afresh, and inflamed her whole being."

**Garden encounter and nature of love**: Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening after recognizing house through Éponine's assistance. Entered garden by forcing old gate; being slender, readily passed through. **At height of love's voluptuousness, Marius remained absolutely chaste—would rather visit woman of town than raise Cosette's robe to ankle height.** **Love described as "chaste, almost shy" yet not devoid of gallantry.** Their conversations made of breaths, murmurs, whispers, childish prattle, laughter at nothing—"everything that is deepest and most sublime in the world." **Authorial reflection**: Love is "life, if it is not death. Cradle; also coffin."

**Confessions of identity (spring Year 6)**: **Cholera decimated Paris during that very month.** They confided as far as possible, but not much further than names. **Marius told Cosette**: orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, lived by writing for publishers, father was colonel and hero, on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. **Cosette told Marius**: brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father's name M. Fauchelevent, very good, gave greatly to poor despite being poor himself.

**Marius's response to departure (late June 1832)**: For last six weeks, Marius slowly taken possession of Cosette. **Upon learning of Valjean's plan to take Cosette to England in one week**: Marius declared this the gravest atrocity imaginable. **Protested he has no money (owes more than ten louis to Courfeyrac), old hat worth three francs, coat missing buttons, shirt ragged, elbows torn, boots leak, cannot afford passport.**

**Cosette's response and final arrangement (late June 1832)**: Cosette agreed not to question further, accepted Marius as her master. Promised to pray, think of him, sing _Euryanthe_ tomorrow evening. **Arranged to meet in garden day after tomorrow at nine o'clock precisely at dusk.** Both fell into each other's arms, lips meeting while uplifted eyes gazed upon stars.

**Marius's oblivion**: Marius's symphony of love since seeing Cosette regularly has rendered recent past so confused that he has completely forgotten nocturnal adventure in hovel, Thénardier, Valjean's burn wound. Does not occur to him to tell Cosette. Both bore languidly the indefinable burden of immaterial pleasures.

## Éponine's Guardianship (Spring Year 6)
**Éponine guards Rue Plumet house against intruders.** On evening of 3d June 1832, towards ten o'clock, Éponine confronts unknown parties (possibly Thénardier and associates): tells them she is there; forbids anyone to enter house; claims she is dog and will bark; says six men don't frighten her; threatens kicks; swears she will be hungry summer and cold winter; displays resolute attitude with elbow on knee, chin in hand, swinging foot with indifference.

## Thénardier's Escape and Accomplices (Winter Year 5)
**Thénardier's escape from Prison Charlemagne**: At two o'clock morning, old sentinel relieved by conscript. At four o'clock, relieving sentinel found conscript asleep. **Thénardier vanished. Hole in cage ceiling and above in roof. One bed plank wrenched off. Half-empty bottle with stupefying wine seized. Soldier's bayonet disappeared.** Reached edge of ruin wall at Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile but strength failed him, separated from street three stories below by steep escarpment.

**Four ruffians' vigil and Gavroche's role**: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, and Montparnasse prowled all night around La Force. **Guelemer seized Gavroche, set him on roof of shanty, handed him rope knotted by Brujon. Gavroche directed steps towards flue. Thénardier bent over wall edge; first light of dawn struck white upon his sweat-dripping brow. Gavroche recognized him.** As soon as Gavroche touched pavement, out of danger, he was no longer weary, chilled, or trembling.

**Brujon and Guelemer's escape**: When Gavroche picked up two lost children, Brujon and Guelemer rose softly and with nail began piercing chimney against which their beds stood. **Successfully escaped.**

## Gavroche and the Two Lost Children (Spring 1832—Spring Year 6)
**Character and rescue**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Stole Montparnasse's purse. Observed two neatly dressed children of unequal stature; barber thrust them back furiously. Gavroche provided bread and promised shelter.

**Elephant shelter**: Led two children through fence gap into elephant enclosure. All three sheltered inside elephant through winter Year 5.

## Father Gillenormand and Marius's Return (Late June 1832)
**Father Gillenormand's character and state**: Well past ninety-first birthday. Lives with Mademoiselle Gillenormand in Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, No. 6. One of those antique old men whom age bears down without bending. Incapable of taking single step towards grandson; would rather die. Placed old portrait of his other daughter (dead), Madame Pontmercy, taken when she was eighteen, opposite head of bed—gazed incessantly at it.

**Evening of 24th June 1832 (before Marius's arrival)**: Alone in chamber, feet propped on andirons, half enveloped in huge screen of coromandel lacquer, elbow on table where burned two candles under green shade, engulfed in tapestry armchair. Thinking of Marius lovingly and bitterly; bitterness predominated. Tenderness once soured always ended by boiling and turning to indignation. Reached point where he tries to accept that which rends his heart. Explaining to himself there was no longer reason why Marius should return. Trying to accustom himself to thought that all was over, he should die without beholding "that gentleman" again. Whole nature revolted; aged paternity would not consent.

**Marius's arrival and awkward reunion**: **After lapse of four years, Marius arrived.** Gillenormand grasped him in single glance. Found him noble, handsome, distinguished, well-grown, complete man. Felt desire to open his arms, call him, fling himself forward; heart melted with rapture. But by contrast which constituted very foundation of his nature, what came forth was harshness. Said abruptly. Would have liked Marius to throw himself into his arms. Displeased with Marius and with himself. Conscious he was brusque, Marius was cold. Caused goodman unendurable and irritating anxiety to feel so tender and forlorn within, only to be able to be hard outside. Bitterness returned. Interrupted Marius in peevish tone.

**Harsh interrogation and announcement**: Gillenormand delivered bitter diatribe comparing youth's advantages (wit, handsomeness, health, teeth, black hair, future full of sunshine, being in love) to old man's infirmities (age ninety-one, losing teeth, legs, memory, losing sight, beloved by no one). Demanded to know why Marius deserted him, left house, drove aunt to despair, led bachelor life, played dandy, came in at all hours, gave no signs of life, contracted debts, became smasher of windows and blusterer. At end of four years comes to him. **Announced he would marry.** Gillenormand reacted with fury: "You marry! At one and twenty! You have arranged that!" Mocked Marius's political allegiances, referenced July Revolution of 1830, cannon-ball in wall of Rue Saint-Antoine. Demanded: "Whom? Can one inquire without indiscretion?" **Upon learning her name related to Fauchelevent/Pousselevent, declared absolutely: "Never, sir, never!"**

**Sudden reversal**: At tone in which "never" was uttered, Marius lost all hope. Traversed chamber with slow steps, bowed head, tottering like dying man. Gillenormand followed with eyes. At moment Marius was on point of going out, Gillenormand advanced four paces with senile vivacity, seized Marius by collar, brought him back energetically, flung him into armchair. **There was now something so kind, so gentle, so openhearted, and so paternal in this brusqueness, that Marius, in sudden transition from discouragement to hope, was stunned and intoxicated.**

**Marius's confession of love**: Seated near table, light from candles brought out dilapidation of costume, which Gillenormand regarded with amazement. Marius passionately declared: "Father, my good father, if you only knew! I love her. You cannot imagine it; the first time I saw her was at the Luxembourg...in the beginning, I did not pay much heed to her, and then, I don't know how it came about, I fell in love with her. Oh! how unhappy that made me! Now, at last, I see her every day, at her own home, her father does not know it, just fancy, they are going away, it is in the garden that we meet, in the evening, her father means to take her to England, then I said to myself: 'I'll go and see my grandfather and tell him all about the affair. I should go mad first, I should die, I should fall ill, I should throw myself into the water. I absolutely must marry her, since I should go mad otherwise.' She lives in a garden with an iron fence, in the Rue Plumet. It is in the neighborhood of the Invalides."

## Thénardiers and Child Substitution
**Family disruption**: Thénardiers imprisoned following Jondrette garret arrest.

**Magnon arrangement**: Before police raid, Thénardier handed two little sons to Magnon (fashionable woman in criminal sphere). Magnon promised ten francs monthly, actually paid. M. Gillenormand (grandfather) continued compact. Children well cared for.

**Spring 1832 dispersal**: Shortly after police raid, Magnon and Mamselle Miss seized. **Two children set out alone, elder leading younger, holding paper with address M. Barge, Rue du Roi-de-Sicile, No. 8. Gust of wind tore paper from elder's fingers; unable to find it as night fell. Lost in city, wandering in spring cold.**

## Provincial Details (Winter Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**Deaths and transfers**: Ulrald Corrford died of old age at Staveford. **Silver flute and amber map (which Ulrald Corrford owned) went to Kassa Brackick.** Provincial characters and observations: Vesmira, Luvie Prydenridge, Isvie Stenworth, Marald Corrford, Fenelle Lindmere, Elra Corrford, Bremira, Yedan Corrford, Ferald Stenworth, Thizek, Thizek Stenenridge, Lura, Rimor, Rimor Corrford, Kassa, Kassa Brackick, Kassa Stenson, Rozek, Rozek Stenenridge, Luena, Luena Stenenridge, Lurald Stenworth, Rorald Lindmere, Pelde Stenworth. Activities: Rimor watched clouds and predicted rain wrongly. Kassa laughed at story nobody else found funny. Kassa Stenson hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step. Rimor complained of aching back. Rimor argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Elra fell asleep in chair before fire caught. **Elra Corrford told Isvie she looked tired.** Ferald Stenworth and Marald Corrford discussed salt prices. **Marald hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step.** **Lurald Stenworth walked long way round to avoid muddy square.** **Elra Corrford argued with carter over price of sack of oats.** **Rozek and Luena Stenenridge talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.** **Rozek fell asleep in chair before fire had caught.** **Rozek spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight.** **Rozek Stenenridge gave copper chalice to Luena.** **Rozek Stenenridge argued with carter over price of sack of oats.** **Luena fell asleep in chair before fire had caught.** **Luena walked long way round to avoid muddy square.** **Rozek Stenenridge remarked river is up again; Luena said it always was in spring.** Frost silvered hedges overnight. Smoke lay flat over fields. Gulls quarreled over fish heads. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Carts creaked past wells.

## Authorial Philosophy (Chapters 20-21)
**Progress versus past**: "The past is very strong...Let us sell the field on which Hannibal is encamped." Progress and future: "When they say 'no' to progress, it is not the future but themselves that they are condemning...There is but one way of rejecting To-morrow, and that is to die."

**Social philosophy and remedy**: Society must heed how it breathes. **"Social phthisis called misery."** Intellectual and moral growth indispensable as material improvement. "To know is sacrament, think is prime necessity, truth is nourishment as well as grain."
